Retrieval augmented generation for clinical question answering evaluates how retrieved evidence can reduce unsupported answers in medical workflows.
The recorded parser fixture represents text extracted from an open-access PDF and keeps enough prose to exercise parser diagnostics without calling a live PDF source.
The study describes retrieval pipelines, citation grounding, abstract evidence, full text evidence, evaluation protocols, and limitations of clinical deployment.
Researchers compare answer faithfulness, citation coverage, retrieval ranking, and safety caveats across several biomedical question answering tasks.
The paper reports that evidence quality depends on source selection, parser quality, and whether the model receives relevant passages instead of noisy document fragments.
Clinical users need transparent warnings when extracted text is short, empty, scanned, corrupted, or dominated by non-text artifacts.
For this fixture, the parser should count words and characters, retain normalized whitespace, produce a stable hash, and attach diagnostics that downstream storage can inspect.
The fixture also includes enough ordinary alphanumeric prose to avoid a low-quality classification while still allowing tests to simulate an empty second page.
Production ingestion should use these diagnostics to avoid silently treating weak PDF extraction as reliable full text evidence.
Recorded parser fixtures make the behavior repeatable in continuous integration, independent of arXiv rate limits, network timeouts, or PDF parser dependency changes.
